title: Hidden Repeat in 1 to n
statement:
You get an array nums of length n + 1. Every value is a whole number from 1 to n. By the pigeonhole principle at least one value must repeat; here exactly one value repeats, and it may appear two or more times. Every other value appears at most once.

Return the repeated value.

The rules that make it interesting: do not modify nums (no sorting it, no marking entries), and use only O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: n = 6, seven slots, values 1 to 6. Only 6 appears twice.
n = 4, and 2 fills every slot while 1, 3 and 4 are missing. "Sum of the array minus 1 + 2 + … + n" gives 10 − 10 = 0 here, so that trick only works when the repeat appears exactly twice.
n = 5, and 5 appears three times while 4 is missing. XOR or sum tricks break as soon as a value is missing.

constraints: Exactly one value appears more than once
hints: A set solves it in one pass but uses O(n) memory. Since values are between 1 and n, they could also be used as positions in the array. What happens if you treat nums[i] as "go to index nums[i] next"?
Follow i → nums[i] starting from index 0. Nothing points back to index 0, because no value is 0. The walk can never end. So what shape does it have, and which index has two arrows pointing at it?

It is a linked list with a loop, and the repeated value is where the loop starts. Find it with Floyd: slow and fast pointers until they meet, then restart one pointer at index 0 and move both one step at a time. They meet at the loop entry.

explain.intuition:
Read the array as a linked list: index i is a node, and nums[i] is its next pointer. Every value is between 1 and n, so every pointer leads to a valid index, and nothing ever points back to index 0. Start at index 0 and follow pointers. The walk never stops, and there are only n + 1 nodes, so it must eventually run into a loop.

The node where the loop starts is special: two different nodes point at it, the one just before it on the path and the last node of the loop. Two indices holding the same pointer means two equal values in nums. So the loop entry is the repeated value, and finding a loop entry with O(1) memory is exactly Floyd's cycle algorithm.

Why does phase two work? Say the path from index 0 to the entry has length a, and the slow pointer met the fast one b steps into the loop of length c. Fast has walked twice as far as slow, so the extra distance it covered is a whole number of laps: a + b = k·c. So from the meeting point, another a steps land exactly on the entry, and that is also what a steps from index 0 do.
steps: Phase 1: slow = nums[0], fast = nums[nums[0]]. While they differ, move slow once and fast twice.
Phase 2: set slow = 0 and leave fast at the meeting point.
While slow !== fast, move each one step: slow = nums[slow], fast = nums[fast].
Return slow, the loop entry, which is the repeated value.
pitfalls: Returning the meeting point of phase 1. That is some node inside the loop, not necessarily its entry.
Starting phase 2 from nums[0] instead of index 0. Both pointers must be exactly a steps from the entry, and the path is measured from index 0.
Using the sum or XOR trick. It assumes the repeat appears exactly twice and nothing is missing, which the second and third examples break.

solutions.title: Remember what you have seen
solutions.idea: Scan once and keep a set. The first value already in the set is the repeat. Simple and O(n), but it breaks the O(1) memory rule.

solutions.title: Binary search on the value
solutions.idea: Count how many entries are ≤ mid. If more than mid, the repeat is in 1..mid (pigeonhole); otherwise it is above mid. O(1) memory, no changes to nums.

solutions.title: Array as a linked list (Floyd)
solutions.idea: Treat i → nums[i] as next pointers from index 0. The walk ends in a loop whose entry has two incoming pointers, so it is the repeated value. Floyd's algorithm finds it.

followups: If you were allowed to modify the array, how could you find the repeat in O(n) time and O(1) memory by marking entries?
Why does the walk have to start at index 0 and not at any other index?
